newsitem.title: UK: Japan's forex rethink meets deafening U.S. silence.
newsitem.headline: Japan's forex rethink meets deafening U.S. silence.

text.p: Japanese authorities raced on Friday to repair the damage inflicted on the dollar by fears that the world's three biggest economies may be losing their appetite for a strong U.S. currency. But soothing comments from heavyweights like Japan's prime minister and finance minister failed to convince the markets and analysts said the silence from the U.S. spoke volumes.
"The longer the silence persists the more the markets will gain the impression that the U.S. is aquiescing to the dollar's decline," said Tim Fox, economist at Standard Chartered Bank.

Influential Japanese Ministry of Finance (MOF) official Eisuke Sakakibara was quoted on Thursday as saying dollar/yen's correction of last year's plunge was about to end and the finance ministry was not trying to weaken the yen further.
Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr Yen" for his part in dragging the unit down from last year's post-war high against the dollar, also said Japan's economy was stronger than the markets thought.

But new finance minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Friday that Japanese interest rates were likely to stay low and echoed Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's assertion that the economy was recovering, though only gradually. "Japan wanted to see the yen weaken substantially to help their recovery, but I think in their minds enough is enough and they'll be happy to see dollar/yen stabilise around 110," said Howard Archer, research manager at National Westminster Bank.
The dollar has appreciated sharply from the post World War II low of 79.70 yen it hit last April, climbing to touch a 3-1/2-year peak of 114.91 on October 29 this year.
Sakakibara's comments hauled dollar/yen back from levels above 114, and it scraped a low of 111.26 in Europe on Thursday. It was quoted at 112.08 yen by 1207 GMT on Friday.

But economists said Japan had wished to stabilise and cap dollar/yen rather than drastically weaken it. Sakakibara caught out a market which had been monitoring the U.S. for any sign it might retreat after Tuesday's presidential election from its oft-stated commitment to a strong dollar.
U.S. industry has made no secret of its dissatisfaction with dollar strength, and the market fears the administration could now start paying more heed to that.
Analysts said, however, that a dollar level of 100 to 110 yen should satisfy business communities in both the U.S. and Japan, giving the U.S. every reason to remain tight-lipped now.

"The complaints about the weaker yen have usually come from the U.S. Now the Japanese have to a degree indicated where they'd like dollar/yen to be, I suspect the U.S. is quite happy with that," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi.

Germany, however, is unlikely to welcome a weaker dollar. A stronger mark is the last thing authorities there want as it risks strangling the fragile German export-led recovery and destabilising the whole process of European monetary union.
Dollar/yen's slump on Friday did unsettle dollar/mark but to a lesser extent, analysts noted. The dollar lost around a pfennig and was trading near 1.51 marks at 1250 GMT on Friday.

"To the extent there's not been a massive move in dollar/mark they can afford to stay on the sidelines," said Shepperd. A deeper downturn would concern the Germans, though Japanese-style comments are not their stkle and interest rate cuts are unlikely right now, he said.
"It's not clear what the Germans can do except keep their fingers crossed and hope the mark tends to weaken."
